title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: Every $d$-regular graph $G$ on $n$ vertices contains a spanning subgraph $H$ so that for every $k$, $0 \leq k \leq d$, $\left|m(H, k) - \frac{n}{d+1}\right| \leq 2$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. For a graph $H$ and an integer $k\ge0$, $m(H,k)$ denotes the number of vertices of degree $k$ in $H$, and $m(H)=\max_k m(H,k)$ is the maximum number of vertices of the same degree; a small value of $m(H)$ measures the irregularity of $H$ (every graph with at least two vertices has $m(H)\ge2$). If $G$ is $d$-regular on $n$ vertices, every spanning subgraph has degrees in $\{0,\dots,d\}$, so $m(H)\ge\frac{n}{d+1}$ by pigeonhole; the conjectures say that every graph has a spanning subgraph nearly as irregular as its degrees permit. If true, both conjectures (this one and its companion for minimum degree, resp. for $d$-regular graphs) are tight: the disjoint union of two $4$-cycles is an example, and an extra additive $1$ is needed even when $\frac{n}{d+1}$ is an integer, e.g. when $\lfloor\frac{d+1}{2}\rfloor\frac{n}{d+1}$ is odd, by parity of the number of odd-degree vertices. The authors could not prove it, but show an asymptotic version: if $d^3\log n=o(n)$, every $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices has a spanning subgraph $H$ with $m(H,k)=(1+o(1))\frac{n}{d+1}$ for all $0\le k\le d$; in general they get a spanning subgraph with $m(H)\le8\frac nd+2$.

title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta$ contains a spanning subgraph $H$ satisfying $m(H) \leq \frac{n}{\delta+1} + 2$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. For a graph $H$ and an integer $k\ge0$, $m(H,k)$ denotes the number of vertices of degree $k$ in $H$, and $m(H)=\max_k m(H,k)$ is the maximum number of vertices of the same degree; a small value of $m(H)$ measures the irregularity of $H$ (every graph with at least two vertices has $m(H)\ge2$). If $G$ is $d$-regular on $n$ vertices, every spanning subgraph has degrees in $\{0,\dots,d\}$, so $m(H)\ge\frac{n}{d+1}$ by pigeonhole; the conjectures say that every graph has a spanning subgraph nearly as irregular as its degrees permit. If true, both conjectures (this one and its companion for minimum degree, resp. for $d$-regular graphs) are tight: the disjoint union of two $4$-cycles is an example, and an extra additive $1$ is needed even when $\frac{n}{d+1}$ is an integer, e.g. when $\lfloor\frac{d+1}{2}\rfloor\frac{n}{d+1}$ is odd, by parity of the number of odd-degree vertices. The authors could not prove it, but show that every graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta$ has a spanning subgraph $H$ with $m(H)\le(1+o(1))\lceil\frac{n}{\delta+1}\rceil+2$ (with $o(1)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$), and with $m(H)\le\lceil\frac{n}{\delta+1}\rceil+2$ if $\delta^{1.24}\ge n$ and $n$ is large; in general they get $m(H)\le16\frac{n}{\delta}+4$. The companion conjecture for $d$-regular graphs asks for a spanning $H$ with $|m(H,k)-\frac{n}{d+1}|\le2$ for every $0\le k\le d$.
